headline: A tomb guard yelled at Hegseth. The Pentagon agreed.
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, his wife and senior aides posed for photos at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington on Veterans Day, talking and laughing. The Army sentinel on duty stepped toward them and yelled that visitors keep silence and respect at all times. The Pentagon's spokesman said the soldier was correct. Trump praised Hegseth that day.

cover_question.q: Can a soldier yell at the boss?

cover_answer: Yes. At that tomb, the rule is the rule for everyone.
table_question: Would you call out your boss for breaking a rule you enforce?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: There is a special grave for a soldier nobody could name, and a guard watches it day and night. The rule there is quiet, like a library. On Wednesday the man in charge of all the soldiers and his friends laughed while taking pictures, and the guard shouted at them to be quiet. His own department said the guard was right.
5-7.why: A six-year-old knows the library rule. One guard, one rule, and the rule won.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reads a parent's face before the words, and a shouting soldier can sound like trouble. The script makes it a rule story: a quiet place, one man keeping it quiet, and the rule holding for the most important visitor. The library is the anchor; they have been shushed there. Expect 'did he get in trouble?' No. The department said he did his job.

8-12.script: Since 1948 a soldier has guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, and the rule is silence. On Veterans Day, Pete Hegseth, who runs the Pentagon, posed for photos there and someone laughed. The sentinel yelled the rule at them. The Pentagon backed him: a league upholding the referee's call.
8-12.why: A rule, the top guy breaking it, and the rule enforced anyway.
8-12.why_long: At ten they are testing whether adults apply rules to themselves, so the script gives them a clean case: one rule since 1948, the top official breaking it, and a soldier enforcing it on him. The referee is the mechanism, and the Pentagon's statement is the league backing the call. Expect 'will the soldier get punished?' The Pentagon said he was correct.

13-17.script: Does a rule mean more when it is enforced on the defense secretary? A sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier yelled at Pete Hegseth and his aides for laughing through a photo, and the Pentagon said the soldier was correct. Second: does a short video change your view of him, or confirm it?
13-17.why: Two true things: the rule held, and the man it held against lost nothing.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the rule held against the man who runs the Pentagon, and nothing happened to him for it. The script asks whether enforcement is the point when it changes nothing, and whether a short video is evidence or a mirror for what they thought. Expect 'why is this news?' The Pentagon put in writing that the guard was right.

5-7.q: Can a soldier yell at the boss?
5-7.a: At that tomb, yes. His job is to keep it quiet and respectful for everyone, and his own department said he got it right.

8-12.q: Who is buried in that tomb?
8-12.a: A soldier killed in World War I whose name nobody knows.
Nothing in the report. The Pentagon said the soldier was correct.

13-17.q: Did the Pentagon really side against its own boss?
13-17.a: Its spokesman said the soldier was "correct." He did not name Hegseth.

13-17.q: Did Hegseth get in any trouble?
13-17.a: No. Trump praised him that day. An impeachment vote had just failed.
